title: David J.P. O’Sullivan
text:
ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR · STATISTICS & DATA ANALYTICS
I am an Associate Professor in the Department of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Limerick, and a member of the Mathematics Applications Consortium for Science and Industry (MACSI).
My research focuses on the science of social networks. I develop analytical tools to understand how network structure affects the spread of information and behaviour — for example, whether fake news spreads differently than a virus — the social mechanisms behind the emergence of behaviours on networks, and how online networks shape and reflect public deliberation, such as the polarised opinion groups that formed around Irish referendums on Twitter/X. I am also keenly interested in applying statistical methods to real-world industry problems.

title: ECMI blog on our work
text:
Dear reader, my PhD student, Caroline Pena, wrote an ECMI blog about our work. It focused on our recent work that was published in RSOS. In the work we collected and analysed a large corpus of Twitter data that dealt with the Irish abortion referendum to understand how different groups communicated online and how information spread inside and between those groups. You can find the blog post here.
The paper in question can be found here.

title: Research
text:
NETWORKS · DISEASE CONTAGION · SOCIAL CONTAGION · COMPUTATIONAL SOCIAL SCIENCE
My primary research focuses on the science of social networks, such as Facebook or Twitter/X. I develop analytical and computational tools across four connected strands:

title: Research
text:
Structure and spreading
How does network structure affect the spread of information and behaviour? Does fake news spread differently than a virus like COVID-19? I use generating-function methods, multitype branching processes, and simulation to model simple and complex contagion on clustered networks (including practical questions such as the effectiveness of contact tracing when networks contain cliques).
Related work: A generating-function approach to modelling complex contagion on clustered networks (J. Complex Networks, 2023); Effectiveness of contact tracing on networks with cliques (Phys. Rev. E, 2024); Modeling diffusion in networks with communities (Phys. Rev. E, 2025).

title: Research
text:
Emergence of behaviour on networks
What social mechanisms allow different behaviours to emerge and stabilise on networks? I study how local interaction rules aggregate into population-level phenomena.

title: Research
text:
Networks and public deliberation
Social networks both shape and reflect online and real-world debate around public deliberative processes. A running theme in my work is the Irish referendum context, for example, the polarised opinion groups that formed on Twitter/X around the marriage and abortion referendums, and how information diffused within and between those groups.
Related work: Finding polarized communities and tracking information diffusion on Twitter: A network approach on the Irish Abortion Referendum (R. Soc. Open Sci., 2025).

title: Research
text:
Identifying attitude groups
Networks can be used to identify groups holding differing attitudes from behavioural and survey data, connecting network methods with social psychology.

title: Research
text:
Applied statistics for industry
Through MACSI, I am keenly interested in the application of statistical methods to real-world problems for industry. If you have an industry problem that could benefit from statistical or network modelling, I’d be glad to hear from you.
